jhmt-2020-calculus-01.title: Fourth derivative and AM-GM
jhmt-2020-calculus-01.body:
The fourth derivative of $f$ is $f''''(x) = (\sqrt{2})^4 e^{x\sqrt{2}} = 4e^{x\sqrt{2}}$. So
$$\frac{f''''(x)}{f(x)} = \frac{4e^{x\sqrt{2}}}{x^2 + e^{x\sqrt{2}}} \le \frac{4e^{x\sqrt{2}}}{e^{x\sqrt{2}}} = 4,$$
with equality when $x^2 = 0$, i.e.~$x = 0$. The maximum value is $\boxed{4}$.

jhmt-2020-calculus-02.title: Substitution and L'Hôpital
jhmt-2020-calculus-02.body:
Substitute $u = 1/x$ so the limit becomes
$$\lim_{u\to 0} \frac{\sqrt{1+120u+121u^2} - \sqrt{1+20u+21u^2}}{u}.$$
By L'Hôpital's rule, differentiate numerator and denominator with respect to $u$ and evaluate at $u = 0$:
$$\frac{(120 + 242u)/(2\sqrt{1+120u+121u^2}) - (20+42u)/(2\sqrt{1+20u+21u^2})}{1}\Bigg|_{u=0} = \frac{60}{1} - \frac{10}{1} = \boxed{50}.$$

jhmt-2020-calculus-03.title: Critical point via derivative
jhmt-2020-calculus-03.body:
$f'(x) = e^{x\sqrt{3}}(\sqrt{3}\sin x + \cos x)$. Setting $f'(x) = 0$ gives $\sqrt{3}\sin x + \cos x = 0$, so $\tan x = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$. On $(0, \pi)$, this yields $x = 5\pi/6$.

Since $f'(x) > 0$ on $(0, 5\pi/6)$ and $f'(x) < 0$ on $(5\pi/6, \pi)$, the transition point is $a\pi/b = 5\pi/6$, giving $a = 5$, $b = 6$. Thus $a + b = \boxed{11}$.

jhmt-2020-calculus-04.title: Symmetry about pi
jhmt-2020-calculus-04.body:
Since $\frac{\cos^3x}{\cot x}=\cos^2x\sin x$, the integrand equals $e^{\cos x}\cos^2x\sin x+1$, so
$$\int_{\pi-1}^{\pi+1}\left(e^{\cos x}\cos^2x\sin x+1\right)dx=2+\int_{\pi-1}^{\pi+1}g(x)\,dx,\qquad g(x)=e^{\cos x}\cos^2x\sin x.$$
Because $\cos(2\pi-x)=\cos x$ and $\sin(2\pi-x)=-\sin x$, we have $g(2\pi-x)=-g(x)$: $g$ is odd about $x=\pi$, so its integral over the symmetric interval $[\pi-1,\pi+1]$ is $0$. The integral equals exactly $2$, and the answer is $\boxed{2}$.

jhmt-2020-calculus-05.title: Orthogonality of pursuit
jhmt-2020-calculus-05.body:
By symmetry the four robots always form a square. If robot $A$ chases robot $B$, then $A$'s velocity points along $\overrightarrow{AB}$, while $B$'s velocity points along the next side of the square, which is perpendicular to $\overrightarrow{AB}$. So $B$'s motion never changes the distance $AB$ to first order; the gap shrinks only through $A$'s own motion, at exactly $A$'s speed.

Hence the length of $A$'s path equals the amount by which the distance $AB$ has decreased. That distance starts at $100$ and tends to $0$ as the robots spiral into the center but stays positive, so each path length approaches $100$ without exceeding it. The smallest such integer is $L=\boxed{100}$.

jhmt-2020-calculus-06.title: Infinity norm is the max absolute value
jhmt-2020-calculus-06.body:
The infinity norm equals $\max_{1\le k\le 10}|u_k|$. The quadratic $u_k = 2020 + 202k - 20k^2 = -20(k^2 - \frac{202}{20}k) + 2020$ has its maximum at $k = \frac{202}{40} = 5.05$, so $k = 5$ gives the maximum among integers.

Compute $u_5 = 2020 + 202(5) - 20(25) = 2020 + 1010 - 500 = 2530$. All entries are positive for $k = 1, \ldots, 10$ (verify $u_{10} = 2020 + 2020 - 2000 = 2040 > 0$). So $\|\vec{u}\|_\infty = \max|u_k| = u_5 = \boxed{2530}$.

jhmt-2020-calculus-07.title: Limit definition of e
jhmt-2020-calculus-07.body:
$999999^{1000000} = (10^6 - 1)^{10^6} = (10^6)^{10^6}\left(1 - 10^{-6}\right)^{10^6}$. The factor $(10^6)^{10^6}$ just shifts the decimal point; the leading digits come from $\left(1 - 10^{-6}\right)^{10^6}$.

Since $\lim_{n\to\infty}(1 - 1/n)^n = e^{-1} = 1/e$, and $n = 10^6$ is large enough that $(1 - 1/n)^n \approx 1/e$ to three decimal places, the leading digits of $1/e = 0.36787\ldots$ are $3, 6, 7$. Thus $A = 3$, $B = 6$, $C = 7$, and $100A + 10B + C = \boxed{367}$.

jhmt-2020-calculus-08.title: Pattern of repeated derivatives
jhmt-2020-calculus-08.body:
Define $g_n(x) = f(x)x^{-n}$. One can show by induction that any derivative $f^{(z)}(x)$ is a linear combination of $\{g_1(x), g_2(x), \ldots, g_{2z}(x)\}$ with a nonzero $g_{2z}(x)$ coefficient.

Therefore $f^{(2020)}(x) = \frac{f(x)(c + xP(x))}{x^{4040}}$ for some polynomial $P$ and constant $c \ne 0$, giving
$$\frac{x^k f^{(2020)}(x)}{f(x)} = x^{k-4040}(c + xP(x)).$$
This limit is $0$ as $x \to 0^+$ precisely when $k > 4040$, so the smallest such integer is $k = \boxed{4041}$.

jhmt-2020-calculus-09.title: Rationalizing
jhmt-2020-calculus-09.body:
The condition is $\frac1n>3-2\sqrt[4]5$, and $3-2\sqrt[4]5>0$ since $(2\sqrt[4]5)^4=80<81$. Rationalizing twice,
$$(3-2\sqrt[4]5)(3+2\sqrt[4]5)=9-4\sqrt5,\qquad(9-4\sqrt5)(9+4\sqrt5)=81-80=1,$$
so the condition is $n<(3+2\sqrt[4]5)(9+4\sqrt5)$.

With $\sqrt5\approx2.23607$ and $\sqrt[4]5\approx1.49535$, this product is about $5.9907\times17.9443\approx107.50$. So the largest integer $n$ is $\boxed{107}$.

jhmt-2020-calculus-10.title: Substitution and arctan integral
jhmt-2020-calculus-10.body:
Substitute $u = \cos x$, $du = -\sin x\,dx$, and use $x = \cos^{-1}(u)$:
$$\int_0^\pi \frac{x\sin x}{1+\cos^2 x}dx = \int_1^{-1} \frac{\cos^{-1}(u) \cdot (-du)}{1+u^2} = \int_{-1}^{1} \frac{\cos^{-1}(u)}{1+u^2}du.$$
Using $\cos^{-1}(-u) + \cos^{-1}(u) = \pi$:
$$= \pi\int_0^1 \frac{du}{1+u^2} = \pi\left[\arctan u\right]_0^1 = \pi \cdot \frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{\pi^2}{4}.$$
So $a = 4$, $b = 2$, and $10a + b = \boxed{42}$.

jhmt-2020-calculus-11.title: Logarithmic derivative
jhmt-2020-calculus-11.body:
Write $P(x)=a\prod_{j=1}^d(x-r_j)$. By the product rule, for $x$ not a root,
$$\frac{P'(x)}{P(x)}=\sum_{k=1}^d\frac{1}{x-r_k}.$$
Taking $x=3$: $P(3)=3^2+20\cdot3-20=49\ne0$ and $P'(3)=2\cdot3+40=46$, so
$$\sum_{k=1}^d\frac{1}{3-r_k}=\frac{P'(3)}{P(3)}=\frac{46}{49},$$
already in lowest terms. The answer is $46+49=\boxed{95}$.

jhmt-2020-calculus-12.title: Triple-angle identity and telescoping
jhmt-2020-calculus-12.body:
Using $\sin(3\theta) = 3\sin\theta - 4\sin^3\theta$, we get $\sin^3\theta = \frac{3\sin\theta - \sin(3\theta)}{4}$. With $\theta = \pi/3^n$:
$$3^n\sin^3\!\left(\frac{\pi}{3^n}\right) = \frac{3^n}{4}\left(3\sin\frac{\pi}{3^n} - \sin\frac{\pi}{3^{n-1}}\right) = \frac{3}{4}\left(3^n\sin\frac{\pi}{3^n} - 3^{n-1}\sin\frac{\pi}{3^{n-1}}\right).$$
The sum telescopes:
$$\sum_{n=1}^{100} 3^n\sin^3\!\left(\frac{\pi}{3^n}\right) = \frac{3}{4}\left(3^{100}\sin\frac{\pi}{3^{100}} - 3^0\sin\pi\right) = \frac{3}{4}\cdot 3^{100}\sin\frac{\pi}{3^{100}}.$$
For very small $\theta$, $\sin\theta \approx \theta$, so $3^{100}\sin(\pi/3^{100}) \approx \pi$. Thus $100 \cdot \frac{3\pi}{4} \approx 75\pi \approx 235.6$, and the greatest integer is $\lfloor 75\pi \rfloor = \boxed{235}$.
